learner.troublesome: Two price drivers move at once: the index and IV. The learner's direction call can be right while the trade still loses, which feels unfair and invites outcome-based conclusions.

misconceptions.statement: If the direction is right, a bought option makes money.
misconceptions.correction: The move must beat the move already priced in; an IV fall and time decay can outweigh a right-direction move.
misconceptions.reasoning: The playbook states 'Direction alone is not a thesis', and the case trainee's written thesis is direction-only, so the desk expects this error.

misconceptions.statement: A trade's profit or loss shows whether the decision was good.
misconceptions.correction: Judge the decision by the process that was knowable at entry; outcomes are noisy.
misconceptions.reasoning: Outcome bias is documented in general populations (S-3); the desk rule EV-6.1 exists to counter it.

teaching.canDo: Before buying premium into a scheduled event, estimate the implied move and write why your expected move beats it, or record no trade.
teaching.keyIdea: Implied volatility rises into an event and crushes after it, so a right direction only pays if the move beats the implied move.
teaching.selfExplainPrompt: Why did the trainee's call lose money even though the index rose?

explanation.text: Implied volatility is the volatility that makes the pricing model match an option's market price. Before a scheduled event it usually climbs, because the outcome is unknown, and after the announcement it usually falls within minutes: the IV crush. A call bought the day before therefore carries that uncertainty in its premium. A right direction is not enough; the move must beat the implied move, which the desk estimates from the ATM straddle. In the case, the index rose 110 points against a priced move of about 304, and the IV fall cost more than the move earned. Rule EV-2.1 asks you to write why your expected move beats the implied move, or to choose no trade.

walkthrough.say: The IV crush is the quick fall in implied volatility once the announcement removes the uncertainty.

walkthrough.target: the move must beat the implied move

example.title: A trainee's event-day call (illustrative paper trade)
example.scenario: A trainee bought 4 lots of the 24200 call at 90.25 rupees the day before a policy announcement. The index rose 110 points, IV fell from 17.5% to 11%, and the call closed at 59.55.
example.takeaway: The priced move was about 304 points; a 110 point rise could not pay for the premium once IV crushed.

workedQuestion.prompt: Before an event, the ATM 24050 call is 153.55 and the put is 150.75. Your thesis expects a 150 point rise. Estimate the implied move and say what EV-2.1 tells you to do.
modelAnswer: Implied move: 153.55 + 150.75 = 304.30, so about plus or minus 304 points.
My expected move of 150 points is smaller than the implied move of about 304 points.
Under EV-2.1 I cannot say why my move beats the implied move, so I record no trade, or wait until IV resets after the announcement.

checks.prompt: What usually happens to implied volatility right after a scheduled announcement?
options: It usually falls quickly
It usually rises further
It stays the same until expiry
It moves only with the index direction

distractorRationale.It usually rises further: error: confuses the run-up before the event with the reaction after it
distractorRationale.It stays the same until expiry: error: thinks IV only changes at expiry

checks.explanation: Once the outcome is known the uncertainty is gone, so IV usually falls within minutes: the IV crush. It climbs before the event, not after.

checks.prompt: A trainee's note before a policy announcement says only 'Policy will be positive, index will go up. Bought calls.' Under EV-2.1, what is missing?
options: A stronger reason why the index will rise
Why the expected move beats the implied move
The previous day's closing price
A bigger position to cover the cost
checks.answer: Why the expected move beats the implied move

distractorRationale.The previous day's closing price: error: lists data that does not change the decision
distractorRationale.A bigger position to cover the cost: error: sizes from conviction, which the desk forbids

checks.explanation: EV-2.1 asks for the size of the move, not only its direction. A stronger direction argument still says nothing about whether the move beats the roughly 304 points already priced.

checks.prompt: The index rose 110 points, but the call lost 30.70 rupees per unit. The screen reads Move +40, IV -48, time -23. What mainly caused the loss?
options: The index moved the wrong way
Brokerage and other charges
The fall in IV after the event
The strike was below spot
checks.answer: The fall in IV after the event

distractorRationale.Brokerage and other charges: error: the P&L shown is before charges
distractorRationale.The strike was below spot: error: misreads moneyness; 24200 is above the 24040 spot

checks.explanation: The move earned 40 rupees per unit, but the IV fall took 48 and time took 23. The direction was right; the IV crush was the largest cost.

checks.prompt: Before the event, the ATM 24050 call is 153.55 and the put is 150.75. Roughly what move is the market pricing by expiry?
options: About 304 points either way
About 154 points either way
About 110 points either way
About 31 points either way

distractorRationale.About 154 points either way: error: used one leg of the straddle only
distractorRationale.About 110 points either way: error: used the realised move, which was not known at entry

checks.explanation: 153.55 + 150.75 = 304.30, so the desk's quick guide puts the implied move near 304 points. The 110 point move only became known after the event.

checks.prompt: An event-day trade lost money, but the pre-trade note was complete, followed EV-2.1 and stayed inside the event budget. How should the desk review it?
options: Bad trade: tighten the rule that allowed it
Lucky escape: the loss could have been bigger
Skip the review because the loss was inside budget
Good process, bad outcome: repeat the process
checks.answer: Good process, bad outcome: repeat the process

distractorRationale.Lucky escape: the loss could have been b: error: confuses the process and outcome quadrants
distractorRationale.Skip the review because the loss was ins: error: EV-6.1 reviews every trade on process

checks.explanation: EV-6.1 judges process, not P&L. A complete note with a loss is the cost of the odds; calling it a bad trade is outcome bias.

checks.prompt: In two sentences the desk lead can read in the morning meeting, explain why the trainee's call lost money even though the index rose.

sentences.english: The implied volatility of an option is the volatility that, put into the pricing model, gives its market price.
Before a scheduled event, implied volatility usually climbs, because the market is paying for an outcome nobody knows yet.

title.en: Why the right direction is not enough

sentences.english: After the announcement the uncertainty is gone, and implied volatility usually falls within minutes; the desk calls this the IV crush.
An option bought the day before the event has that uncertainty built into its premium.
So a right direction is not enough: the index must move more than the implied move to pay for the premium.
The desk's quick guide is that the ATM straddle price approximates the implied move by expiry.
Rule EV-2.1 says: if you cannot explain why your expected move beats the implied move, do not buy premium into the event.
